newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Weak Swedish crown puts brakes on rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Weak Swedish crown puts brakes on rate cuts.

text.p: The Swedish crown is likely to eventually recover some of the ground lost in its recent slide, but in the short term it will remain volatile, preventing the central bank from cutting rates, analysts said on Tuesday.
The crown has softened 6.8 percent since last October and is running at a year low against the mark, which analysts said could temporarily halt the central bank's easing trend.

"To cut rates the Riksbank would have to distance itself from the crown as an inflation indicator, but the crown has always been an important monetary indicator," Peter Granqvist, a Swedbank bond and currency analyst, said.
"We'll see on Thursday (when the central bank presents its latest quarterly inflation report) how the Riksbank interprets the crown weakening."
Over the past 15 months the Riksbank has followed an aggressive monetary policy, cutting its key interest rate, the repo, 25 times last year to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent.
However, the bank has not cut the repo rate since December 17.
Analysts said the Riksbank would probably like to keep lowering rates as the economic fundamentals were strong, but the weak and volatile crown was blocking such a move.

At 1230 GMT on Tuesday, the crown was changing hands at 4.5900 to the mark, softening from 4.5680 late on Monday and 4.5745 on Friday when worries about a possible delay to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) put the skids under the unit.
"The crown is influenced by the daily talk about EMU and could weaken to 4.65 to the mark in the next few days," said Thomas Ryve, Midland Bank's head of treasury and capital.
In general, market players flee to the mark when fears arise over whether the EMU will start on schedule in 1999, as the monetary union is expected to support all currencies except the mark.

The crown is also suffering from signs the minority Social Democratic government, whose support has fallen sharply in recent polls, will loosen the purse strings ahead of Sweden's next general election in September 1998.
The Social Democrats have traditionally safeguarded the welfare state, but since taking power in 1994 they have implemented tight fiscal policies and cut benefits to try to improve state finances.
With expectations of a budget surplus in 1998, Prime Minister Goran Persson has started talking about putting 10 billion crowns ($1.3 billion) into the public sector.

While market worries have driven the crown lower, fundamentals are sturdy with strong state finances, a year-on-year negative inflation figure of 0.4 percent in February and a 1996 current account surplus of 41.5 billion crowns.
"Fundamentals do not speak for higher Swedish short bond yields and a weaker crown, but fundamentals do not have any impact, speculation rules," Ryve said.
In the long term, after the government's spring budget proposal on April 15 and its party congress in September, the crown should strengthen if EMU worries subside, analysts said.
"We see the crown trading at 4.40-4.35 to the mark within three months," said Marie Giertz, economist at Handelsbanken.
Granqvist said the crown could rebound from its recent lows but found it hard to see what would reverse the longterm negative trend which has prevailed since November 1996.
"I do absolutely not believe that the crown will reach 6.65 against the dollar and 4.25 to the mark, levels it traded at three or four months ago," he said.
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 7.738 Swedish Crowns)
